requirements.requirement: On node1, allow only root and opsadmin to schedule cron jobs.
requirements.summary: The final /etc/cron.allow contains exactly root and opsadmin with root ownership and mode 0600. Both users were observed as authorized, opsadmin successfully installed and listed a crontab, daemon was explicitly denied, test crontabs were removed, and the same behavior persisted after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel, using software compatible with the platform.
requirements.summary: Before and after execution, node1 remained RHEL 10.0 on kernel 6.12.0-55.9.1.el10_0.x86_64. Package health remained intact, and the existing cronie package provided the implementation.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied. The node-wide restart protocol is also complete: healthy pre-restart state and boot identity were captured, reboot was acknowledged, the post-restart boot identity changed, and the system, crond service, configuration, access behavior, and empty test spool recovered. Fixed lifecycle observations independently corroborate the boot transition.
limitations: Unauthorized access was behaviorally sampled with the daemon account rather than every possible local account; the exact two-entry allow-list supplies coherent supporting evidence that all unlisted users are excluded.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. Creating opsadmin and /etc/cron.allow directly established the required access policy; temporary crontabs and output files were bounded verification artifacts and were removed. The reboot was required by the provider-wide evidence protocol. Final observations show no failed services, new exposure, package damage, or abandoned temporary artifacts; reboot-related PID and systemd-private-directory changes are normal lifecycle effects.
